- **Key finding 3**: Correction magnitude control is critical and previously unrecognized — norm=1.42 yields 0%, norm=0.1-0.2 yields +7pp, obs_only CRM is uniquely robust across the magnitude range.

---

## 1. Introduction (~1.5 pages)

### Motivation
- VLAs (π₀, OpenVLA, SmolVLA) represent a paradigm shift in robot learning, but distribution shift remains a major challenge.
- LIBERO benchmark exposes robustness gap: VLA performance degrades significantly under object/spatial perturbations.

### Gap

- **RL-based refinement** (SC-VLA): requires per-task RL training, not plug-and-play.

2. **Systematic conditioning comparison + honest negative result**: Per-DOF conformal statistics — intuitively richer features — provide no CRM benefit. Observation features suffice. This challenges synthetic-experiment intuition and reveals the gap between per-step MSE and closed-loop success.
3. **Correction magnitude sensitivity**: First empirical study of correction magnitude control for VLA action refinement. obs_only CRM is robust across norms; perdof CRM collapses at high correction magnitudes.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\paragraph{VLA Robustness Methods.}
5	Recent work has sought to improve the robustness of vision-language-action models through training-time interventions.
6	SRPO~\cite{srpo2025} applies self-referential reinforcement learning to fine-tune VLA policies, achieving strong gains on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark.
7	RobustVLA~\cite{robustvla2025} combines RL post-training with Jacobian regularization to stabilize action predictions under visual perturbations.
8	DiG-Flow~\cite{digflow2025} introduces discrepancy-guided flow matching, steering the generative process toward more accurate denoising trajectories during training.
9	SnapFlow~\cite{luan2026snapflow} distills multi-step flow-matching into single-step inference, reducing latency while preserving action quality.
10	TT-VLA~\cite{liu2026ttvla} adapts VLA parameters at test time via reinforcement learning, blurring the line between training-time and inference-time approaches.
11	VLA-GSE~\cite{vla_gse_2026} improves generalization through parameter-efficient fine-tuning with gated sparse experts, and Cosmos-Policy~\cite{cosmos_policy_2026} leverages video foundation models for visuomotor control.
12	These methods are complementary to ACR-VLA: they improve the base policy itself, whereas ACR-VLA operates as a post-hoc inference-time module that attaches to any frozen flow-matching VLA without modifying its weights.
13	This orthogonality means ACR-VLA can be composed with any of the above methods to provide additional robustness through uncertainty-conditioned correction.
14	
15	\paragraph{Uncertainty Quantification for Robot Learning.}
16	Quantifying predictive uncertainty in learned policies is essential for safe deployment.
17	Deep Ensembles~\cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} and MC-Dropout~\cite{gal2016dropout} are foundational approaches that estimate epistemic uncertainty through multiple forward passes or stochastic weight perturbations, but both produce scalar or loosely structured uncertainty estimates that do not distinguish which action dimensions are uncertain.
18	In the generative policy setting, Diffusion Policy~\cite{chi2023diffusion_policy} introduced the diffusion-based action generation paradigm that flow-matching VLAs build upon; its stochastic sampling naturally admits multi-sample uncertainty estimation, though the original work does not exploit this for correction.
19	DiU~\cite{xing2026diu} shows that for flow-matching models, the divergence of the velocity field recovers per-DOF \emph{aleatoric} uncertainty from a single forward pass, providing an efficient uncertainty signal without additional sampling.
20	ACR-VLA differs along two axes.
21	First, it estimates \emph{model uncertainty} via multi-sample covariance---a sampling-based signal that reflects both epistemic and aleatoric components, and that rises under distribution shift when the policy is uncertain about the correct action---which we find more actionable for correction than single-pass aleatoric estimates (validated in ablation A7).
22	Second, it produces a structured 40-dimensional feature vector (per-DOF standard deviations, calibrated conformal radii, and log-volume) rather than a scalar summary, enabling dimension-selective correction as demonstrated in Section~\ref{sec:motivating}.
23	
24	\paragraph{Conformal Prediction in Robotics.}
25	Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees and has seen growing adoption in robotics.
26	\citet{angelopoulos2023gentle} provide a comprehensive tutorial on the framework.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{VLA Robustness Methods.}
Recent work has sought to improve the robustness of vision-language-action models through training-time interventions.
SRPO~\cite{srpo2025} applies self-referential reinforcement learning to fine-tune VLA policies, achieving strong gains on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark.
RobustVLA~\cite{robustvla2025} combines RL post-training with Jacobian regularization to stabilize action predictions under visual perturbations.
DiG-Flow~\cite{digflow2025} introduces discrepancy-guided flow matching, steering the generative process toward more accurate denoising trajectories during training.
SnapFlow~\cite{luan2026snapflow} distills multi-step flow-matching into single-step inference, reducing latency while preserving action quality.
TT-VLA~\cite{liu2026ttvla} adapts VLA parameters at test time via reinforcement learning, blurring the line between training-time and inference-time approaches.
VLA-GSE~\cite{vla_gse_2026} improves generalization through parameter-efficient fine-tuning with gated sparse experts, and Cosmos-Policy~\cite{cosmos_policy_2026} leverages video foundation models for visuomotor control.
These methods are complementary to ACR-VLA: they improve the base policy itself, whereas ACR-VLA operates as a post-hoc inference-time module that attaches to any frozen flow-matching VLA without modifying its weights.
This orthogonality means ACR-VLA can be composed with any of the above methods to provide additional robustness through uncertainty-conditioned correction.

Quantifying predictive uncertainty in learned policies is essential for safe deployment.
Deep Ensembles~\cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} and MC-Dropout~\cite{gal2016dropout} are foundational approaches that estimate epistemic uncertainty through multiple forward passes or stochastic weight perturbations, but both produce scalar or loosely structured uncertainty estimates that do not distinguish which action dimensions are uncertain.

DiU~\cite{xing2026diu} shows that for flow-matching models, the divergence of the velocity field recovers per-DOF \emph{aleatoric} uncertainty from a single forward pass, providing an efficient uncertainty signal without additional sampling.

First, it estimates \emph{model uncertainty} via multi-sample covariance---a sampling-based signal that reflects both epistemic and aleatoric components, and that rises under distribution shift when the policy is uncertain about the correct action---which we find more actionable for correction than single-pass aleatoric estimates (validated in ablation A7).

The most closely related line of work addresses action refinement at inference time without retraining the base policy.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

% Para 1: Problem — VLA success + robustness gap under distribution shift
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) that generate actions via flow matching~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla} have reached 97--99\% success rates on standard manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO~\cite{liu2023libero}.
Yet this near-saturation masks a fragile reality: under distribution shifts common in real-world deployment---camera viewpoint changes, lighting variation, sensor noise, object layout differences---the same policies suffer substantial performance degradation~\cite{fei2025liberoplus}.
Closing this robustness gap is a prerequisite for deploying learned manipulation policies outside tightly controlled lab settings.

% Para 2: Existing approaches — training-time vs inference-time, what they miss
Two lines of work address VLA robustness.
\emph{Training-time methods} improve the base policy itself: SRPO~\cite{srpo2025} applies self-referential policy optimization, while RobustVLA~\cite{robustvla2025} and DiG-Flow~\cite{digflow2025} incorporate robustness-aware objectives into training.
These methods are effective but require retraining or fine-tuning, and their gains are bounded by the training distribution.
\emph{Inference-time methods} leave the policy frozen and intervene at deployment.
ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} draws multiple action samples and selects the one closest to the sample mean, using scalar Euclidean distance as an uncertainty proxy.
SAFE~\cite{gu2025safe} detects anomalous states and triggers fallback behaviors.
UPS~\cite{yuan2026ups} and CP-in-the-Loop~\cite{wang2025cploop} use conformal prediction for binary decisions---execute or abstain, safe or unsafe---but do not use conformal statistics as features for continuous correction.
A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns a residual correction that runs asynchronously alongside the base policy, yet applies it without uncertainty conditioning, lacking any mechanism to modulate correction magnitude across action dimensions.
In short, no existing method performs inference-time action correction conditioned on \emph{structured, per-degree-of-freedom uncertainty}.

% Para 3: Our insight — per-DOF conformal features as continuous input to learned correction
Our key observation is that the stochastic samples already produced by a flow-matching VLA contain rich, structured uncertainty information that current methods discard.
By fitting a shrinkage-regularized Gaussian to $K{=}10$ samples and computing multivariate conformal statistics~\cite{braun2025cgs}, we obtain a 40-dimensional feature vector that encodes \emph{which} action dimensions are uncertain (per-DOF standard deviations), the \emph{calibrated confidence level} (conformal radii from Adaptive Conformal Inference~\cite{gibbs2021aci}), and the \emph{overall predictive spread} (log-volume of the covariance ellipsoid).
This representation captures substantially more structure than the scalar distances used in ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla}: it preserves the cross-DOF covariance structure that enables a downstream module to correct high-uncertainty dimensions aggressively while leaving confident predictions untouched.
A controlled 3D point-reaching experiment confirms this: a correction MLP conditioned on per-DOF uncertainty reduces total error by 6.7\% over scalar conditioning and by 16.7\% over no uncertainty input, with 22--24\% improvements concentrated on the non-perturbed axes where scalar conditioning cannot distinguish signal from noise (Section~\ref{sec:motivating}).

% Para 4: ACR-VLA overview — 3 components, key design choices
We introduce \textbf{ACR-VLA} (Adaptive Conformal Refinement for VLA), an inference-time module that attaches to any frozen flow-matching VLA and performs dimension-selective action correction.
ACR-VLA comprises three components:
(i)~\textbf{Conformalized Gaussian Scoring (CGS)} draws $K{=}10$ samples per control step, fits a Ledoit--Wolf shrinkage covariance, and extracts a 40D structured uncertainty feature;
(ii)~\textbf{Adaptive Conformal Inference with Chunk Overlap Consistency (ACI+COC)} maintains an online conformal threshold~\cite{gibbs2021aci} using a self-referential coverage signal derived from overlapping action chunks---requiring no external supervisor, reward model, or ground-truth actions;
(iii)~\textbf{Conformal Refinement Module (CRM)}, a lightweight MLP (${\sim}$337K parameters) that takes the CGS features as conditioning and outputs a dimension-selective residual correction.
We note that conformal prediction serves here as a \emph{feature extraction and calibration mechanism}, not as a guarantee on the corrected output: CGS features provide structured uncertainty conditioning for CRM, while ACI+COC adapts these features online under distribution shift.
We instantiate ACR-VLA on SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla}, a 450M-parameter flow-matching VLA.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Per-DOF conformal features for dimension-selective correction.}
  We show that the 40D CGS representation---per-DOF standard deviations, calibrated conformal radii, and covariance log-volume---enables CRM to selectively correct uncertain action dimensions while preserving accurate ones.
  On LIBERO, ACR-VLA improves base SmolVLA success by \textbf{XX.X}\,pp, and ablations confirm that per-DOF features outperform both scalar uncertainty and no-uncertainty baselines (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

  \item \textbf{Self-referential online calibration via Chunk Overlap Consistency.}
  COC exploits the temporal overlap in receding-horizon action chunks to provide a coverage signal for ACI without external supervision.
  This enables the conformal threshold to adapt online under arbitrary distribution shift, maintaining calibrated uncertainty features throughout deployment (Section~\ref{sec:aci}).

  \item \textbf{Systematic evaluation across multiple LIBERO task suites.}
  We evaluate ACR-VLA on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object, providing per-task breakdowns, ablations isolating the contribution of each component (CGS features, ACI+COC calibration, CRM architecture), and analysis of when and why dimension-selective correction helps (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

% --- Para 1: VLAs are impressive but fragile under distribution shift ---
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) that generate actions via flow matching~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} have reached 97--99\% success rates on standard manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO~\cite{liu2023libero}.
Yet this near-saturation masks a fragile reality: distribution shifts routinely encountered in deployment---object substitution, spatial layout changes, lighting variation---can degrade success rates by 30--50 percentage points~\cite{fei2025liberoplus}.
Closing this robustness gap without retraining the base policy is a prerequisite for deploying VLAs outside tightly controlled settings.

% --- Para 2: Existing approaches and the gap ---
Two lines of work address VLA robustness.
\emph{Training-time methods} improve the base policy itself through robustness-aware objectives~\cite{srpo2025,robustvla2025,digflow2025} or test-time reinforcement learning~\cite{liu2026ttvla}.
These approaches are effective but require retraining or per-task RL, and their gains are bounded by the training distribution.
\emph{Inference-time methods} leave the policy frozen.
ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} draws multiple action samples and selects the most conforming one, but sample selection is fundamentally limited: it cannot produce an action better than the best candidate in the sample set.
VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} applies evolutionary optimization over action samples, but incurs 2.41\,s per control step---too slow for real-time manipulation.
A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns an asynchronous residual correction, but applies it unconditionally without first selecting a high-quality starting action.
In short, no existing inference-time method combines statistical sample selection with learned action correction on a frozen VLA.

% --- Para 3: Our approach — sample-then-correct ---
We introduce \textbf{ACR-VLA} (\textbf{A}daptive \textbf{C}onformal \textbf{R}efinement for VLA), an inference-time module that improves frozen VLA actions through a \emph{sample-then-correct} pipeline.
At each control step, ACR-VLA draws $K{=}10$ action samples from the frozen VLA, selects the most conforming candidate via Mahalanobis-based nonconformity scoring with shrinkage covariance estimation~\cite{ledoit2004well,braun2025cgs}, and then applies a learned residual correction via a lightweight \emph{Conformal Residual Module} (CRM).
CRM is a 329K-parameter MLP conditioned on the VLA's frozen observation embedding.
It predicts a small residual $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ whose $L_2$ norm is clipped to a bound $\varepsilon$, producing the corrected action $\mathbf{a}^* = a_{\mathrm{base}} + \mathrm{clip}(\boldsymbol{\delta})$.
The critical design insight is that correction operates on a high-quality starting point---the conformal-selected action---and that bounding the correction magnitude prevents compounding errors from destabilizing the closed-loop trajectory.
The base VLA is never modified; ACR-VLA attaches as a post-hoc module to any frozen flow-matching VLA.

% --- Para 4: Key findings (with exp_id references) ---
We evaluate ACR-VLA on LIBERO-Object (10 tasks, 100 trials per method) and LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks, 100 trials) using SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} as the frozen backbone. Three findings emerge:

\textbf{(1)~Sample-then-correct outperforms sample-then-select.}
On LIBERO-Object, observation-conditioned CRM achieves 19.0\% success versus 12.0\% for conformal selection alone---a +7.0 percentage point improvement representing a 58\% relative gain.
% exp_id: eval-acr-object-v4-obs-only (19.0%), eval-argmin-only-object (12.0%)
% TODO: update with pooled seed=42+43 results and Fisher exact p-value
Averaging all $K$ samples (VLA-mean) or using a single sample (VLA-only) both yield 12.0\%, confirming that the gain comes from learned correction, not from increased sampling alone.
% exp_id: eval-vla-only-object-k1 (12.0%), eval-vla-mean-object (12.0%)

\textbf{(2)~Observation features suffice for correction; conformal features do not help.}
Counter to intuition from synthetic experiments, conditioning CRM on per-DOF conformal statistics (perdof: 11.0\%) performs no better than selection alone (12.0\%), while scalar conformal conditioning (9.0\%) is actively harmful.
% exp_id: eval-acr-object-v4-small (perdof 11.0%), eval-acr-object-v4-scalar (9.0%)
Only observation-conditioned CRM (19.0\%) produces meaningful improvement.
This honest negative result highlights a gap between per-step prediction accuracy---where richer features help in offline evaluation---and closed-loop task success, where covariance estimation noise from $K{=}10$ samples undermines per-DOF conditioning.

\textbf{(3)~Correction magnitude control is critical and previously unrecognized.}
Without magnitude bounding, the CRM's natural output ($\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_2 \approx 1.42$) causes catastrophic failure: 0\% success, as compounding correction errors rapidly drive the state distribution away from the CRM's training regime.
Constraining corrections to $\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_2 \leq 0.1$ recovers the full +7.0\,pp gain.
% exp_id: eval-acr-spatial-v4-default-r3 (norm=1.42, 0%), eval-acr-object-v4-obs-only (norm=0.1, 19.0%)
Observation-conditioned CRM maintains stable 35--36\% success on LIBERO-Spatial across $\varepsilon \in [0.05, 0.3]$, while per-DOF-conditioned CRM collapses from 35\% to 26\% over the same range---further evidence that observation features provide more robust conditioning for learned correction.
% exp_id: eval-mag-obsonly-norm005, eval-mag-obsonly-norm03, eval-mag-perdof-norm03

We note that correction offers targeted improvements on object-centric manipulation rather than universal gains: on LIBERO-Spatial, all CRM variants perform within ${\pm}1$\,pp of selection alone, suggesting that the correction mechanism is most effective when distribution shift induces systematic action biases that a learned module can identify and compensate.

% --- Para 5: Contributions ---
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{A sample-then-correct pipeline for frozen VLAs.}
  We propose ACR-VLA, the first system to combine conformal sample selection with learned residual correction for frozen flow-matching VLAs.
  On LIBERO-Object, this pipeline improves SmolVLA success by +7.0\,pp over selection alone.
  % TODO: update with pooled seed results and p-value: (p < 0.05 on combined 200 trials, Fisher exact test)

  \item \textbf{Systematic conditioning comparison and honest negative result.}
  We compare three CRM conditioning variants---per-DOF conformal features, scalar uncertainty, and observation features---and find that only observation conditioning is effective.
  This challenges the intuition that richer uncertainty features should yield better corrections, and reveals that covariance estimation noise at $K{=}10$ undermines per-DOF conditioning in closed-loop settings.

  \item \textbf{First empirical study of correction magnitude sensitivity for VLA action refinement.}
  We show that unbounded correction causes catastrophic failure and that observation-conditioned CRM is uniquely robust across a $6{\times}$ range of magnitude bounds ($\varepsilon \in [0.05, 0.3]$), establishing magnitude control as a critical design axis for inference-time action correction.
\end{enumerate}

  We show that unbounded correction causes catastrophic failure and that observation-conditioned CRM is uniquely robust across a $6{\times}$ range of magnitude bounds ($\varepsilon \in [0.05, 0.3]$), establishing magnitude control as a critical design axis for inference-time action correction.
\end{enumerate}
